sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description:
Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

Codemode: `tools.edit(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description:
Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

Codemode: `tools.write(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: codemode
toolsAdded.description:
Run JavaScript that calls other tools. The input is raw JavaScript (not JSON, no code fence), run as an async function body in a QuickJS sandbox: top-level `await` and `return` work. No Node, file system, network, or timers.
- `await tools.<name>({ ...args })` resolves to a string, or an object if the tool's declaration says so, and rejects with an Error on failure. A tool whose declaration returns an object resolves on failure too when it returned that object; check its fields. Calls still running when the script ends are cancelled.
- Optional first line: `// @options: {"max_output_tokens": 10000, "timeout_ms": 60000}`

Globals:
- `text(value)`, `image(dataUrlOrImageBlock)`, `console.log(...)`, and top-level `return` add output; `exit()` ends the script. With several text items, each starts with a `==> text N/M <==` line, and `console` lines follow the other output in one `<console_output>` block. `image()` also saves the image to a temp file and the result names its path.
- `store(key, value)` and `load(key)` keep JSON values across codemode calls.
- `ALL_TOOLS`, `await searchTools(query, { limit?, namespace? })`, `await describeTool(name)`, `await describeNamespace(name)`: find unlisted tools, such as MCP tools.

# Pool Worker

You are a pool worker agent in a Gas City workspace. You were spawned
because work is available. Find it, execute it, close it, and exit.

Your agent name is `$GC_AGENT`. Your session ID is `$GC_SESSION_ID`.

## GUPP — If you find work, YOU RUN IT.

No confirmation, no waiting. You were spawned with work. Run it.
When you're done, exit. The reconciler will spawn a new worker when
more work arrives.

## Startup Protocol

Find and claim your work with the hook. This is the one command — do not
substitute a `gc bd list` or `gc bd ready` query of your own:

```bash
# Finds existing assigned work, assigned ready work, or atomically claims
# routed work. If nothing is available, it acknowledges runtime drain.
gc hook --claim --drain-ack --json
```

If the result action is `work`, read the returned `bead_id` with
`gc bd show <id>`. If the result action is `drain`, the drain was
acknowledged for you: your session is done — exit.

**Never look for your work with `gc bd list --assignee=<your alias>` or
`gc bd ready`.** Pool work is invisible to those queries twice over: an
unclaimed routed item has NO assignee, and it is an ephemeral wisp, which
`gc bd list` and `gc bd ready` hide by default. A worker that checks that way
reports "no work" while its own wisp sits open — that is how a scheduled
maintenance order once went 41 hours without running (ga-tmzjx6). Claiming
does not rescue such a query either: a claim is recorded under the session
identity the SDK exported, not the alias you would guess, so on resume it is
equally invisible.

There is no shorter query to fall back to. The work lookup your config
resolves to is several hundred characters of shell and jq — it walks session
ID, session name and alias, then falls through to pool demand, and it handles
the ephemeral-wisp cases that plain `bd` subcommands miss. `gc hook` exists so
that you never have to reproduce it. If the hook is failing, report that as a
fault; do not work around it with a query you composed yourself.

## Following Your Formula

Your formula defines your work as a sequence of steps. Steps are NOT
materialized as individual beads — they exist in the formula definition.
Read the step descriptions and work through them in order.

**THE RULE**: Execute one step at a time. Verify completion. Move to next.
Do NOT skip ahead. Do NOT claim steps done without actually doing them.

On crash or restart, re-read your formula steps and determine where you
left off from context (last completed action, git state, bead state).

**Never use wide filesystem searches when a CLI command exists.** Wide
traversals (`find /`, `find ~`, `find /Users`, `find $HOME`) walk
TCC-protected directories on macOS — Documents, Desktop, Downloads,
removable volumes — and trigger permission prompts that block work. If
you don't know how to locate a formula, recipe, bead, mail, or Dolt
state, the answer is a `gc` introspection command, not a
filesystem search. If no command exists for what you need, file a bead.

## Molecules — STOP, check BEFORE you start working

**CRITICAL:** When you run `gc bd show` in step 4, look at the METADATA
section. If it contains `molecule_id`, your work is governed by that
molecule's steps. Do NOT just read the description and start coding.

Run `gc bd mol current <molecule-id>` to see your steps:

- `[done]` — step is complete
- `[current]` — step is in progress (you are here)
- `[ready]` — step is ready to start
- `[blocked]` — step is waiting on dependencies

**Work one step at a time.** For each `[ready]` step:
1. `gc bd show <step-id>` — read what to do
2. Do the work described in that step
3. `gc bd close <step-id>` — mark it done
4. `gc bd mol current <molecule-id>` — check your position, repeat

Do NOT read the parent bead description and do everything at once.
Do NOT skip steps. Do NOT close steps you didn't execute.

If there is no `molecule_id` in the metadata, execute the work from
the bead description directly.

## Your Tools

- `gc hook --claim --json` — find and atomically claim work
- `gc bd show <id>` — see details of a work item or step
- `gc bd mol current <molecule-id>` — show position in molecule workflow
- `gc bd mol progress <molecule-id>` — show molecule progress summary
- `gc bd close <id>` — mark work or a step as done
- `gc mail inbox` — check for messages
- `gc runtime drain-ack` — end your session (you are ephemeral)

## How to Work

1. Find and claim work: `gc hook --claim --drain-ack --json`
2. If the action is `drain`, exit. If the action is `work`, read `bead_id`.
3. **Check for molecule:** `gc bd show <id>` — look for `molecule_id` in METADATA
4. **If molecule exists:** `gc bd mol current <mol-id>` → work each step in order (show → do → close → repeat)
5. **If no molecule:** execute the work directly from the bead description
6. When all work is done, close the bead: `gc bd close <id>`
7. **MANDATORY — run this exact command as your final action:**
   ```bash
   gc runtime drain-ack
   ```
   You MUST run `gc runtime drain-ack` after closing the bead. This is
   not optional. Without it, you will block other work from being picked
   up. Do NOT say "drained" without actually running the command. Do NOT
   output any text after running it.

## Escalation

When blocked, escalate — do not wait silently. `human` is the reserved
recipient alias that resolves in every city; if your city staffs a
coordinator role (e.g. the gastown pack's mayor), mail that instead:

```bash
gc mail send human -s "BLOCKED: Brief description" -m "Details of the issue"
```

## Context Exhaustion

If your context is filling up during long work:

```bash
gc runtime request-restart
```

This blocks until the controller restarts your session. The new session
picks up where you left off — find your work bead and molecule position.


## Skills available to this session

You are `cmu-database-group-lectures/pi-2`. The following skills are materialized in your provider's skill directory and load automatically — you don't need to invoke anything extra.

- `core.gc-agents` — Managing agents — list, peek, nudge, suspend, drain *(core)*
- `core.gc-city` — City lifecycle — status, start, stop, init *(core)*
- `core.gc-dashboard` — API server and web dashboard — config, start, monitor *(core)*
- `core.gc-dispatch` — Routing work to agents with gc sling and formulas *(core)*
- `core.gc-mail` — Sending and reading messages between agents *(core)*
- `core.gc-rigs` — Managing rigs — add, list, status, suspend, resume *(core)*
- `core.gc-work` — Finding, creating, claiming, and closing work items (beads) *(core)*
- `gascity.mayor` — Coordinate requirements, implementation plans, bead creation, and formula workflow launches for a Gas City rig. Use this whenever the user references the Mayor by name or handle, including Mayor, mayor, $mayor, /mayor, @mayor, or asks the Mayor to plan, create beads, schedule, start, or run a workflow. *(gascity)*

# Notes for marimo Notebooks

marimo uses Python to create notebooks, unlike Jupyter which uses JSON. Here's an example notebook: 

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = [
#     "marimo",
#     "numpy==2.4.3",
# ]
# requires-python = ">=3.14"
# ///

import marimo

__generated_with = "0.20.4"
app = marimo.App(width="medium")


@app.cell
def _():
    import marimo as mo
    import numpy as np

    return mo, np


@app.cell
def _():
    print("hello world")
    return


@app.cell
def _(np, slider):
    np.array([1,2,3]) + slider.value
    return


@app.cell
def _(mo):
    slider = mo.ui.slider(1, 10, 1, label="number to add")
    slider
    return (slider,)


@app.cell
def _():
    return


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

```

Notice how the notebook is structured with functions can represent cell contents. Each cell is defined with the `@app.cell` decorator and the inputs/outputs of the function are the inputs/outputs of the cell. marimo usually takes care of the dependencies between cells automatically. 

## Running Marimo Notebooks

```bash
# Run as script (non-interactive, for testing)
uv run <notebook.py>

# Run interactively in browser
uv run marimo run <notebook.py>

# Edit interactively
uv run marimo edit <notebook.py>
```

## Script Mode Detection

Use `mo.app_meta().mode == "script"` to detect CLI vs interactive:

```python
@app.cell
def _(mo):
    is_script_mode = mo.app_meta().mode == "script"
    return (is_script_mode,)
```

## Key Principle: Keep It Simple

**Show all UI elements always.** Only change the data source in script mode.

- Sliders, buttons, widgets should always be created and displayed
- In script mode, just use synthetic/default data instead of waiting for user input
- Don't wrap everything in `if not is_script_mode` conditionals
- Don't use try/except for normal control flow

### Good Pattern

```python
# Always show the widget
@app.cell
def _(ScatterWidget, mo):
    scatter_widget = mo.ui.anywidget(ScatterWidget())
    scatter_widget
    return (scatter_widget,)

# Only change data source based on mode
@app.cell
def _(is_script_mode, make_moons, scatter_widget, np, torch):
    if is_script_mode:
        # Use synthetic data for testing
        X, y = make_moons(n_samples=200, noise=0.2)
        X_data = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32)
        y_data = torch.tensor(y)
        data_error = None
    else:
        # Use widget data in interactive mode
        X, y = scatter_widget.widget.data_as_X_y
        # ... process data ...
    return X_data, y_data, data_error

# Always show sliders - use their .value in both modes
@app.cell
def _(mo):
    lr_slider = mo.ui.slider(start=0.001, stop=0.1, value=0.01)
    lr_slider
    return (lr_slider,)

# Auto-run in script mode, wait for button in interactive
@app.cell
def _(is_script_mode, train_button, lr_slider, run_training, X_data, y_data):
    if is_script_mode:
        # Auto-run with slider defaults
        results = run_training(X_data, y_data, lr=lr_slider.value)
    else:
        # Wait for button click
        if train_button.value:
            results = run_training(X_data, y_data, lr=lr_slider.value)
    return (results,)
```

## State and Reactivity

Variables between cells define the reactivity of the notebook for 99% of the use-cases out there. No special state management needed. Don't mutate objects across cells (e.g., `my_list.append()`); create new objects instead. Avoid `mo.state()` unless you need bidirectional UI sync or accumulated callback state. See [STATE.md](references/STATE.md) for details.

## Don't Guard Cells with `if` Statements

Marimo's reactivity means cells only run when their dependencies are ready. Don't add unnecessary guards:

```python
# BAD - the if statement prevents the chart from showing
@app.cell
def _(plt, training_results):
    if training_results:  # WRONG - don't do this
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
        ax.plot(training_results['losses'])
        fig
    return

# GOOD - let marimo handle the dependency
@app.cell
def _(plt, training_results):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(training_results['losses'])
    fig
    return
```

The cell won't run until `training_results` has a value anyway.

## Don't Use try/except for Control Flow

Don't wrap code in try/except blocks unless you're handling a specific, expected exception. Let errors surface naturally.

```python
# BAD - hiding errors behind try/except
@app.cell
def _(scatter_widget, np, torch):
    try:
        X, y = scatter_widget.widget.data_as_X_y
        X = np.array(X, dtype=np.float32)
        # ...
    except Exception as e:
        return None, None, f"Error: {e}"

# GOOD - let it fail if something is wrong
@app.cell
def _(scatter_widget, np, torch):
    X, y = scatter_widget.widget.data_as_X_y
    X = np.array(X, dtype=np.float32)
    # ...
```

Only use try/except when:
- You're handling a specific, known exception type
- The exception is expected in normal operation (e.g., file not found)
- You have a meaningful recovery action

## Cell Output Rendering


[83 more lines in file. Use offset=201 to continue.]

Marimo only renders the **final expression** of a cell. Indented or conditional expressions won't render:

```python
# BAD - indented expression won't render
@app.cell
def _(mo, condition):
    if condition:
        mo.md("This won't show!")  # WRONG - indented
    return

# GOOD - final expression renders
@app.cell
def _(mo, condition):
    result = mo.md("Shown!") if condition else mo.md("Also shown!")
    result  # This renders because it's the final expression
    return
```

## PEP 723 Dependencies

Notebooks created via `marimo edit --sandbox` have these dependencies added to the top of the file automatically but it is a good practice to make sure these exist when creating a notebook too: 

```python
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = [
#     "marimo",
#     "torch>=2.0.0",
# ]
# ///
```

## marimo check 

When working on a notebook it is important to check if the notebook can run. That's why marimo provides a `check` command that acts as a linter to find common mistakes. 

```bash
uvx marimo check <notebook.py>
```

Make sure these are checked before handing a notebook back to the user. 

**Important**: you have a tendency to over-do variables with an underscore prefix. You should only apply this to one or two variables at most. Consider creating a new variable instead of prefixing entire cells in marimo. 

## api docs

If the user specifically wants you to use a marimo function, you can locally check the docs via: 

```
uv --with marimo run python -c "import marimo as mo; help(mo.ui.form)"
```

## tests 

By default, marimo discovers and executes tests inside your notebook.
When the optional `pytest` dependency is present, marimo runs `pytest` on cells that
consist exclusively of test code - i.e. functions whose names start with `test_`. 
If the user asks you to add tests, make sure to add the `pytest` dependency is added and that
there is a cell that contains only test code.

For more information on testing with pytest see [PYTEST.md](references/PYTEST.md)

Once tests are added, you can run pytest from the commandline on the notebook to run pytest. 

```
pytest <notebook.py>
```

# LanceDB

LanceDB is an embedded vector database that runs in-process (no server to host), persists tables as columnar Lance files on local disk or object storage, and exposes one fluent Python API for vector search, full-text search (FTS / BM25), hybrid search, and SQL-style filters. The same connection works against a local directory, S3/GCS/Azure URIs, or LanceDB Cloud.

**Core mental model:** A `Database` is a directory. Each `Table` is a folder inside it backed by Lance files. You define a schema (often via a Pydantic `LanceModel` whose `Vector` field is wired to an embedding function in the registry), `add()` rows, and call `table.search(...)` to get back a `QueryBuilder` you compose with `.where()`, `.limit()`, `.rerank()`, `.select()`, then materialize with `.to_pandas()` / `.to_list()` / `.to_pydantic()`.

## When to Use

- Building a RAG pipeline that needs a persistent vector store with no separate server
- Combining dense vector search with BM25 full-text search (hybrid) and a reranker
- Storing multimodal data (CLIP / OpenCLIP / Jina) with multiple vector columns per row
- Migrating from Pinecone/Weaviate/Chroma to a file-backed, embedded store
- Running vector search inside a notebook, CLI, Modal job, or serverless function
- Time-travel queries / A-B testing embedding models against the same data
- Upserting via `merge_insert` instead of delete-then-insert
- Driving a vector store from LangChain or LlamaIndex with a uniform backend
- Reading/writing Lance datasets and querying them with DuckDB

## Don't Use For

- Managed multi-tenant search clusters with per-tenant access control — LanceDB Cloud handles this; embedded mode does not
- Transactional OLTP workloads — Lance is columnar, optimized for analytical scans
- Sub-millisecond replicated writes across regions — use a managed service

## Execution Steps for Agents

### Step 1: Install and connect

```python
# uv add lancedb pyarrow pandas pydantic
import lancedb

db = lancedb.connect("./data/lancedb")          # local directory
# db = lancedb.connect("s3://bucket/lancedb/")  # object storage
# db = lancedb.connect("az://container/lancedb/")
# db = lancedb.connect("db://my-project", api_key="sk_...", region="us-east-1")  # Cloud

# Async variant — only when you need it (async iteration, FastAPI, etc.)
# db = await lancedb.connect_async("./data/lancedb")
```

A connection is cheap; you can recreate it per request. Don't pre-warm anything.

### Step 2: Define schema with the embedding registry

Prefer the registry pattern — it stores the embedding function with the table, so `add()` and `search()` accept raw text and embed it for you. No bookkeeping.

```python
from lancedb.embeddings import get_registry
from lancedb.pydantic import LanceModel, Vector
```

# Search and Reranking

Every read in LanceDB starts with `tbl.search(...)`, which returns a `QueryBuilder`. Compose modifiers (`.where`, `.limit`, `.select`, `.rerank`, `.nprobes`, `.refine_factor`), then materialize. The same builder handles vector, FTS, and hybrid queries — `query_type` switches the mode.

## The QueryBuilder

```python
qb = tbl.search(query, query_type="vector", vector_column_name="vector")
qb = qb.where("source = 'a.pdf'", prefilter=True)
qb = qb.select(["text", "source"])
qb = qb.limit(10)
qb = qb.nprobes(20).refine_factor(10)        # ANN tuning
qb = qb.rerank(reranker=RRFReranker())       # only meaningful for hybrid / when you set query_string
hits = qb.to_pandas()                         # or .to_list() / .to_arrow() / .to_pydantic(Doc)
```

The chain is lazy. Nothing runs until you call a `to_*` method.

## Vector search

```python
# Pass text → registry-backed table embeds it
hits = tbl.search("contextual retrieval").limit(5).to_pandas()

# Pass a precomputed vector
hits = tbl.search(my_vec).limit(5).to_pandas()
```

Results carry `_distance` (vector mode). Lower is better for `l2`/`cosine`; higher for `dot`. A `_score` column appears in FTS / hybrid results.

### Filtering: prefilter vs postfilter

```python
hits = tbl.search(q).where("source = 'a.pdf'", prefilter=True).limit(5)
```

- `prefilter=True` (recommended for selective predicates) — apply the SQL filter first, then run vector search on the remaining rows. Recall is preserved even when the filter is selective.
- `prefilter=False` (the historical default) — vector search first, then drop hits that fail the filter. Cheap when the filter is broad; can return < `limit` rows when the filter is narrow.

Use `prefilter=True` whenever you have a selective metadata filter — date ranges, tenant scoping, source/category. The performance difference disappears once you `create_scalar_index(column)` on the filtered field.

### ANN tuning at query time

```python
hits = tbl.search(q).nprobes(20).refine_factor(10).limit(10).to_list()
```

- `nprobes` — how many IVF partitions to scan. Default 1; higher means more recall, more latency. 10–20 is a typical starting point on a 256-partition index.
- `refine_factor` — fetch `limit * refine_factor` candidates with the lossy PQ index, then rerank them with full-precision vectors. Default 1 (no refinement); 5–10 buys substantial recall at low cost.

These are the two knobs that matter most for ANN quality. Don't rebuild the index for these — change them at query time.

### Multi-vector tables

```python
tbl.search(q_vec, vector_column_name="text_embedding").limit(5)
tbl.search(q_img, vector_column_name="image_embedding").limit(5)
```

Always pass `vector_column_name` explicitly when the schema has more than one vector column.

## Full-text search (FTS / BM25)

LanceDB ships two FTS backends:

- Native (default in newer versions) — built into the Lance file format, supports incremental updates, scalar prefilter pushdown.
- Tantivy (legacy) — Rust BM25 implementation; requires `pip install tantivy`. Slightly different scoring.

```python
# One-time index — pass the SourceField column name
tbl.create_fts_index("text", replace=True)

# FTS-only query
hits = tbl.search("contextual retrieval", query_type="fts").limit(10).to_pandas()
```

Full-text supports BM25 keyword queries, phrase queries (`"exact phrase"`), boolean operators (`+required -excluded`), and wildcards. Add `replace=True` so reruns don't error.

You can index multiple columns: `tbl.create_fts_index(["text", "title"])`. Specify columns at query time with `.fts_columns(["title"])` or by configuring the index.

## Hybrid search

Hybrid runs both engines, fuses the candidate sets, and lets a reranker order the final list. Always pair with a reranker — the raw fused list is order-arbitrary.

```python
from lancedb.rerankers import RRFReranker

hits = (tbl.search("contextual retrieval", query_type="hybrid")
           .rerank(reranker=RRFReranker())
           .limit(10)
           .to_pandas())
```

Pass a tuple `(vector, text)` when you've precomputed the embedding:
```python
tbl.search((q_vec, "contextual retrieval"), query_type="hybrid").rerank(...).limit(10)
```

Hybrid results contain both `_distance` (vector) and `_score` (FTS) plus a `_relevance_score` injected by the reranker.

## Rerankers

All rerankers live in `lancedb.rerankers`. They take a candidate set (or two — vector and FTS — for hybrid) and produce a final ordering. Wrap any reranker in `.rerank(reranker=R)`.

### Score-fusion rerankers (no model)

These mix existing scores arithmetically — fast, no extra model calls.

```python
from lancedb.rerankers import RRFReranker, MRRReranker, LinearCombinationReranker

RRFReranker()                                                        # reciprocal rank fusion (default for hybrid)
MRRReranker(weight_vector=0.65, weight_fts=0.35)                     # weighted reciprocal-rank
LinearCombinationReranker(weight=0.7)                                # 0 = pure vector, 1 = pure FTS
```

`RRFReranker` is the safe default — bounded, model-free, robust to score scale differences. `LinearCombinationReranker` is intuitive when you want a knob to tune.

### Cross-encoder reranker

Run a sequence-classification cross-encoder over (query, doc) pairs. High quality, much slower than vector/FTS scoring — overfetch and rerank a small top-k.

```python
from lancedb.rerankers import CrossEncoderReranker

reranker = CrossEncoderReranker(model_name="cross-encoder/ms-marco-TinyBERT-L-6")
# 'cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2' is a stronger / slower alternative

hits = (tbl.search(q, query_type="hybrid")
           .rerank(reranker=reranker)
           .limit(10))
```

### Cohere reranker

Hosted reranking via Cohere's API. Strong out-of-the-box quality on multilingual workloads.

```python
from lancedb.rerankers import CohereReranker

reranker = CohereReranker()                                       # default model
# reranker = CohereReranker(model_name="rerank-english-v3.0")
# reranker = CohereReranker(model_name="rerank-multilingual-v3.0")

hits = (tbl.search((q_vec, q_text), query_type="hybrid")
           .rerank(reranker=reranker)
           .limit(10))
```

Set `COHERE_API_KEY` (or pass `api_key=REDACTED

### ColBERT reranker

Late-interaction reranker — embeds the query and each candidate as a list of token vectors, scores by max-over-tokens. Local model, no API key.

```python
from lancedb.rerankers import ColbertReranker
reranker = ColbertReranker()
hits = tbl.search(q, query_type="hybrid").rerank(reranker=reranker).limit(10)
```

### Other rerankers in the wild

- `JinaReranker(api_key=REDACTED — Jina's hosted reranker.
- `OpenaiReranker()` — uses an OpenAI chat model as a judge (slow, expensive, but flexible).
- `FlagEmbeddingReranker(model="BAAI/bge-reranker-base", use_fp16=True)` — popular HuggingFace reranker; the example repo wires it in via `FlagEmbedding.FlagReranker` then sorts by score.

### Custom rerankers

Subclass `lancedb.rerankers.Reranker`. The example repo defines `MofidifiedLinearReranker(LinearCombinationReranker)` to add a hard-filter step before the linear combo:

```python
class TaggedLinear(LinearCombinationReranker):
    def __init__(self, weight: float, filters: list[str]):
        super().__init__(weight=weight)
        self.filters = filters

    def rerank_hybrid(self, query, vector_results, fts_results):
        merged = super().rerank_hybrid(query, vector_results, fts_results)
        keep = merged["text"].apply(lambda t: any(tag in t for tag in self.filters))
        return merged[keep]
```

### Reranker decision table

| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| Default hybrid that "just works" | `RRFReranker()` |
| Tunable dense ↔ sparse mix | `LinearCombinationReranker(weight=0.7)` |
| Highest local quality | `CrossEncoderReranker("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2")` |
| Highest hosted quality, English | `CohereReranker(model_name="rerank-english-v3.0")` |
| Multilingual or low-resource | `CohereReranker(model_name="rerank-multilingual-v3.0")` |
| Local late-interaction | `ColbertReranker()` |
| LLM-as-judge | `OpenaiReranker()` |
| Custom business rules | subclass `Reranker` (or `LinearCombinationReranker`) |

### Vector search + text reranking (without going hybrid)

When you only have a vector but want a text-aware reranker to do the final ordering:

```python
hits = (tbl.search(q_vec)
           .rerank(reranker=CohereReranker(), query_string=q_text)
           .limit(top_k * 2)        # overfetch — reranker keeps the best `limit`
           .to_pandas())
```

Pass `query_string` so the reranker has the natural-language query (vector search alone doesn't give it that).

## Output formats

| Method | Returns | When to use |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `.to_list()` | `list[dict]` | Plain Python; small result sets |
| `.to_pandas()` / `.to_df()` | `pd.DataFrame` | Default in notebooks; use `.iloc`/`.loc` for downstream filtering |
| `.to_arrow()` | `pa.Table` | Hand off to DuckDB / Polars / Parquet |
| `.to_pydantic(Doc)` | `list[Doc]` | Type-safe pipelines (table must have a `LanceModel` schema) |

## Ranking signals attached to results

| Column | When present | Meaning |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| `_distance` | vector / hybrid | similarity distance (lower = closer for L2/cosine) |
| `_score` | FTS / hybrid | BM25 score (higher = more relevant) |
| `_relevance_score` | when `.rerank(...)` is used | reranker's final score (higher = better) |
| `_rowid` | optional, on every result | physical row id; useful for time-travel diffs |

When sorting in app code, prefer `_relevance_score` if you reranked, else `_score` for FTS, else negate `_distance`.

    def generate_embeddings(self, texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]: ...

    date: str
    title: str

    texts: list[str],
    prefix: str,
    embedder: EmbeddingFunction,
) -> list[list[float]]:
    prefixed = [prefix + text for text in texts]
    return [[float(value) for value in vector] for vector in embedder.generate_embeddings(prefixed)]

) -> list[list[float]]:

) -> list[float]:

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

import lancedb
from lancedb.rerankers import MRRReranker

ROOT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT_DIR))  # lecture_search is not an installed package

LANCEDB_REGION = "us-east-1"
TABLE_NAME = "lectures_sample"
TOP_K = 5

    "distributed SQL database replication",
    "YugabyteDB",
]
WEIGHTS_VECTOR = [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]


def load_api_key() -> str:
    env_file = ROOT_DIR / ".env.local"
    if not env_file.exists():
        msg = ".env.local not found"
        raise FileNotFoundError(msg)
    for line in env_file.read_text().splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if line.startswith("LANCEDB_API_KEY=REDACTED
            return line.split("=", 1)[1].strip('"\'')
    msg = "LANCEDB_API_KEY not found in .env.local"
    raise ValueError(msg)


def summarize(rows: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    return [
        {
            "rank": rank,
            "id": row["id"],
            "title": row["title"],
            "text_preview": row["text"][:80].replace("\n", " "),
            **{
                key: round(float(row[key]), 4)
                for key in ("_score", "_distance", "_relevance_score")
                if key in row and row[key] is not None
            },
        }
        for rank, row in enumerate(rows, start=1)
    ]


def main() -> int:
    db = lancedb.connect(LANCEDB_URI, region=LANCEDB_REGION, api_key=REDACTED
    table = db.open_table(TABLE_NAME)
    row_count = table.count_rows()
    print(f"Table {TABLE_NAME}: {row_count} rows")

    # --- Step 1: FTS index on text -------------------------------------
    indices = table.list_indices()
    fts_indices = [
        idx for idx in indices
        if idx.index_type == "FTS" and "text" in (idx.columns or [])
    ]
    if not fts_indices:
        print("FAIL: no FTS index on column 'text'", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    idx = fts_indices[0]
    print(f"FTS index verified: {idx.name} on {idx.columns} "
          f"({idx.num_indexed_rows} indexed rows)")

    report: dict[str, Any] = {"table": TABLE_NAME, "rows": row_count,
                    "fts_index": {"name": idx.name, "columns": idx.columns},
                    "queries": {}}

    for query in QUERIES:
        print(f"\n=== Query: {query!r} ===")
        q_vec = embed_query(query)
        assert len(q_vec) == 768

        entry: dict[str, Any] = {}

        # FTS-only (BM25)
        fts_rows = (
            table.search(query, query_type="fts")
            .limit(TOP_K)
            .to_list()
        )
        entry["fts_only"] = summarize(fts_rows)
        print(f"FTS-only top {TOP_K}: {[r['id'] for r in entry['fts_only']]}")

        # Vector-only
        vec_rows = (
            table.search(q_vec, query_type="vector")
            .limit(TOP_K)
            .to_list()
        )
        entry["vector_only"] = summarize(vec_rows)
        print(f"Vector-only top {TOP_K}: {[r['id'] for r in entry['vector_only']]}")

        # Hybrid with explicit .vector().text() + MRRReranker at 3 weights
        hybrid: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]] = {}
        for w_vec in WEIGHTS_VECTOR:
            w_fts = round(1.0 - w_vec, 1)
            rows = (
                table.search(query_type="hybrid")
                .vector(q_vec)
                .text(query)
                .rerank(MRRReranker(weight_vector=w_vec, weight_fts=w_fts))
                .limit(TOP_K)
                .to_list()
            )
            hybrid[f"vector={w_vec}/fts={w_fts}"] = summarize(rows)
            print(f"Hybrid w_vec={w_vec} w_fts={w_fts}: "
                  f"{[r['id'] for r in hybrid[f'vector={w_vec}/fts={w_fts}']]}")
        entry["hybrid_mrr"] = hybrid

        rank_lists = [tuple(r["id"] for r in rows) for rows in hybrid.values()]
        entry["rankings_differ_across_weights"] = len(set(rank_lists)) > 1

        report["queries"][query] = entry

    out = ROOT_DIR / "data" / "hybrid_verification.json"
    _ = out.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
    print(f"\nFull report written to {out}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Reflex Starter Template

Production-ready [Reflex](https://reflex.dev) starter that deploys to [Railway](https://railway.app) via Docker. The frontend is pre-built into static assets at image build time and served by Caddy; the Reflex backend runs on a separate port and is reverse-proxied for `_event` and `_upload` routes.

This document is written for an autonomous agent. Follow the sections in order. Each command is the literal command to run; do not paraphrase. When a step says "verify", do not skip — stop and report if the check fails.

---

## 1. What gets deployed

- **Frontend**: Next.js static export, built at Docker image build time, served by Caddy on `$PORT` (Railway sets this; defaults to `8080` per `railway.toml`).
- **Backend**: Reflex Python backend on `localhost:8000`, started by `entrypoint.sh`.
- **Reverse proxy**: Caddy proxies `/_event/*`, `/_upload`, and `/_upload/*` to the backend; everything else is served as a static file with SPA fallback to `/404.html`.
- **Health check**: `GET /ping` returns `pong` (used by Railway and the Docker `HEALTHCHECK`).

The split-process model (Caddy + backend, supervised by `entrypoint.sh`) is what lets a single Railway service serve both the static frontend and the WebSocket backend on one port.
